evidence: Abstract: proposes decision-theoretic framework decomposing LLM decision loss into belief formation and belief-to-action components, evaluated on a synthetic benchmark with known ground truth
Section 3: defines R_total = R_belief + R_opt with normalization M(ℓ), distinguishing reported, optimal, and belief-implied actions

Section 6: three domains (synthetic, HailFinder weather, SimSUM clinical), nine threshold loss functions, Qwen3-8B base with separate LoRA adapters per strategy trained via GRPO with eight sampled completions
Appendix E Tables 1-3: intervention deltas vs base with 95% bootstrap CIs; e.g., belief-only ΔR_belief = -0.125±0.014 (HailFinder, independent), decision-only ΔR_total = -0.184±0.019 (HailFinder)

Section 7: claims belief-only training improves beliefs without transferring to decisions; decision-only learns shortcut bypassing belief formation; joint training format-dependent, consistent with tables
Appendix I Table 4: interventions trained on τ∈{0.2,0.4,0.6,0.8} generalize to held-out thresholds with small gaps
Appendix H: reference sensitivity analysis showing mean normalized total regret decreases 18% at d=3 and 25% at d=5 when using empirical frequency instead of true posterior
Discussion: acknowledges single base model for RL, binary-only states, and possible elicitation distortion of reported beliefs
Reproducibility statement: 'All source code will be available on GitHub' - future availability claim only
llm_evaluation.rationale: Strongly on-topic LLM methodology paper: decision-theoretic evaluation of LLM probabilistic reasoning plus targeted RL post-training (Section 5), matching LLM, reasoning, RL/alignment, and evaluation preferences. The regret decomposition R_total = R_belief + R_opt (Section 3) is a clean, well-motivated contribution that differs from prior belief-action coherence work by endowing utility functions and using known reference posteriors (Section 2). Rigor is high: controlled synthetic benchmark with known ground truth (Section 4), matched training controls (same base checkpoint, LoRA+GRPO, Section 6), bootstrap 95% CIs (Appendix E), and three ablations (elicited vs revealed beliefs Appendix G; posterior-reference sensitivity Appendix H; held-out thresholds Appendix I). Evidence is quantitative and consistent with claims: belief-only reduces R_belief (e.g., -0.125±0.014 HailFinder, Table 2) with limited transfer to total regret under independent format; decision-only improves actions without belief gains, supporting the shortcut-policy finding. Weaknesses: RL experiments use a single base model (Qwen3-8B) and binary outcomes (Discussion), some effect sizes are modest (synthetic ΔR_total ≈ -0.03 to -0.06, Table 1), the weather/clinical tasks inherit external benchmarks rather than contributing domain methods, and code availability is only a future claim (Reproducibility statement).

evidence: Abstract: GC-OPD improves mean success over vanilla OPD from 24.70% to 48.78% on ScienceWorld (4B), 53.36% to 85.26% on ALFWorld Unseen, and 29.10% to 37.65% on WebShop with the same original teachers.
Table 1(a): ScienceWorld 1.7B GC-OPD 46.18±1.13 SR exceeds the strongest GRPO-teacher baseline (Vanilla OPD 38.70±0.46); 4B GC-OPD 48.78±0.58 vs 46.66±0.36.

Table 2(a) ablations (ScienceWorld 1.7B): Hindsight-only 31.64%, Minimum-prefix 33.70%, GC success-only 43.68%, full GC 46.18% — isolating contributions of hindsight, graph retrieval, and failed records.
Section 4.1: 'Each trained model is evaluated with four inference seeds at temperature 0.4'; Figure 1(a) caption: '305 tasks, one seed per checkpoint' — no multi-seed training variance reported.
Table 1(b): GC-OPD entries under the Qwen3-32B GRPO teacher condition for ALFWorld are dashes, so the off-the-shelf-vs-GRPO claim is not tested with a GRPO scoring teacher there.
Appendix B.2: state descriptors are environment-specific (ScienceWorld physical-configuration hash, ALFWorld PDDL facts hash, WebShop page/ASIN hashing), requiring manual design per environment.
Appendix C Table 6: K16 collection costs 212.48 GPU-h vs GRPO teacher training 1,169.28 GPU-h; GC-OPD student training 68.79 GPU-h vs vanilla OPD 47.31 GPU-h, supporting the efficiency claim.

Section 3.3 / Appendix B.3: teacher context retains at most one successful and one failed complete source per scored decision with source identities and anchors; full Algorithm B.3 and Table 5 hyperparameters (AdamW, lr 1e-5, clip 0.2, batch 32) are provided.
Title page: code released at https://github.com/hanyi2021/GC_OPD; Appendix A.1 gives model revisions (e.g., Qwen3.5-0.8B at 2fc06364715b).
llm_evaluation.rationale: Highly relevant to top-weighted preferences (LLM agents, on-policy distillation, RL-based teacher training). The method is an incremental but substantive contribution: a source-preserving execution graph that retrieves complete successful/failed records to condition a frozen teacher's token-level scoring, addressing student trajectory divergence. Rigor is strong on baselines (TCOD-B2F/F2B, FTB, TurnOPD under two teacher conditions), ablations (hindsight-only, minimum-prefix, success-only, K budget, generator/scorer swaps), and cost accounting, but weakened by single training runs, SD over only four inference seeds, one-seed validation curves, and missing GC-OPD cells under the GRPO teacher on ALFWorld (dashes in Table 1b). Evidence is detailed and mostly self-consistent (case study probability shift, pass@16 reference, GPU-hour tables), though baseline reproductions are the authors' own. Generalizability is limited by hand-crafted environment-specific state descriptors (Appendix B.2). Reproducibility is good: code link, full hyperparameters, algorithm, and model revisions.

links.title: Delta-Matching: Closing the Final Gap of Native 8-bit Training for LLMs

evidence: Abstract: 'Delta-Matching matches BF16/FP32 mixed-precision training loss and overall downstream performance' and 'We will release our implementation, trained models, and data recipes' (release promised, not yet available).

Section 3.4, Eq. 4–5: proves δ_i^matched = Σ_j P_ij dP̂_ij restores the zero-row-sum invariant under stated numerical assumptions; explicitly builds on 'the direct backward correction (Qiu and Yao, 2026)'.
Section 4.2, Table 1(a): Delta-Matching validation CE 1.4162±0.0006 vs BF16/FP32 1.4178±0.0004; naive stale-delta FP8 1.8970±0.0296; consistent-dO intermediate 1.4667±0.0175 (two seeds).
Section 4.5, Table 4: at 5.29B parameters, naive FP8 CE 1.9327 vs BF16/FP32 1.3349 (RULER-8K 53.5→16.3), Delta-Matching 1.3374±0.0005, demonstrating scale-dependent degradation onset.

Section 4.6: stale-delta loss gap exceeds 0.01 only after ~19,000 steps during 8K-to-64K context extension; Table 5 shows one of two cuDNN/TE FP8 seeds diverged, supporting the error-accumulation claim while noting the confound from the step-18,000 corpus expansion and TE amplitude-history reset.
Appendix C.1, Table 10: instrumented kernel probes show stale-delta pre-cast row-sum residuals 1.1×10⁻²–4.7×10⁻² vs Delta-Matching 1.4×10⁻⁷–7.1×10⁻⁷, rising to 2.7×10⁻³–3.4×10⁻³ after FP8 casting.

Appendix A.4 (Limitations): admits experiments reach only 5.29B/30B tokens, no quantitative law predicting degradation onset, single-initialization Muon study, and timing measurements that 'are not like-for-like training-step comparisons' (Appendix C.2).

Appendix C.5: some architectures (2.58B pure-GQA, Mamba-2/GQA) conceal severe gain corruption (max gain product 878.9/404.1 vs ~2–4 for references) behind near-reference loss — an honest negative-control discussion.

Appendices B.1–B.6: detailed data recipes (Nemotron-CC v2.1 subsets, Llama-2 tokenizer, 0.02 validation holdout), optimizer schedules, precision scopes (Table 7), and full FP8 kernel numerics enabling independent reimplementation.
llm_evaluation.rationale: A core LLM-training-efficiency paper (FP8 attention pretraining), squarely matching the LLM/Transformer/efficiency preferences with no off-scope domain application. The methodological contribution — deriving the stale-delta invariant violation and a matched-delta correction enabling native FP8 in all seven attention-core matmuls — is solid but builds directly on Qiu and Yao (2026)'s earlier BF16/FP32 direct backward correction, so novelty is good rather than exceptional. Rigor and evidence are strong: controlled two-seed comparisons with standard errors, paired validation-loss contrasts over 2,000 windows, kernel-level residual probes (Appendix C.1, Table 10), multiple architectures (GDN/GQA, GDN/MLA, KDA/GQA, Mamba-2/GQA, pure GQA), scales (569M–5.29B), variants, optimizers (AdamW/Muon), and honest ablations of alternative mitigations (Appendix C.4) — with acknowledged confounds (implementation differences, single-seed Muon/auxiliary-output studies, non-like-for-like timing). Generalizability is bounded by the authors' own admission (Appendix A.4) that behavior at substantially larger scales/durations is unestablished and no quantitative law for degradation onset is provided. Reproducibility is excellent in documentation (data recipes, hyperparameters, kernel numerics in Appendices B.1–B.6) though code/model release is only promised, not yet available.

links.title: RLTL;DR: Self-improvement by Internalizing Self-generated Feedback

evidence: Abstract: GRPO stays flat at 0-1% Pass@1 on Pass@128=0 splits while RLTL;DR reaches 12-13% Pass@1 at eval time without insights in context
Section 4.1: GRPO baseline tuned to 72.2% Pass@1 on Appworld test-challenge, near the 73.4% official leaderboard best, supporting baseline quality
Section 5.1: main testbed is a 'proprietary dataset similar to Appworld' with 16k train tasks, limiting external reproducibility
Table 2 (Section 5.2): SFTL;DR deduplicated with 68k backward tokens reaches 16.9% eval Pass@1 vs 20.9% for SFT on 3.5k full rollouts (400M forward tokens), supporting the compacted-training claim
Table 3 (Section 6): removing failed-unit-test access drops eval Pass@1 to 3.4-10.0%; TL;DR format beats diagnostic/summary/code hints for internalization (19.2% vs 16.0-18.6%)
Section 4.2: authors 'refrain from claims on either approach outperforming' regarding RLTF-SD, indicating honest calibration of novelty claims
Figure 2 (Section 4.2): Pass@1 curves averaged across 3 seeds with std; Leetcode acknowledged as likely overfitting
Appendix B: three-step reproduction guide including literal insight-insertion context format, backprop mask editing, and verification checks; Table 4 gives full hyperparameters on 8xB200 nodes
llm_evaluation.rationale: Squarely in-scope LLM-methodology paper: RLVR/GRPO training of a Qwen 3.5 9B agent on tool-calling and coding tasks, using sequential self-generated TL;DR insights plus an SFT loss on (task→insight) tokens to escape the Pass@128=0 learning barrier. High preference relevance (agents, RL, LLMs, code, reasoning). Rigor is strong: deconfounded insight-free metrics, macro-averaging, tuned GRPO baseline (72.2% on Appworld test-challenge, Section 4.1), 3 seeds, and extensive ablations (Tables 2, 3, 8, 9). Evidence is credible but the primary testbed is a proprietary 16k-task 'Synthetic-API' dataset (Section 5.1) and the filtered splits are small (34 Appworld tasks), so external validation is limited. Novelty is moderate: the paper itself frames RLTF-SD as 'similar in kind' and explicitly refrains from outperformance claims (Section 4.2); the striking, well-supported contribution is the SFTL;DR reduction showing (task, insight)-only training nearly matches full SFT (Table 2). Generalizability is partially demonstrated (heldout SAPI/Appworld gains) but Leetcode overfit and the authors flag domain limits (Section 7.2). Reproducibility is hampered by the proprietary dataset and no stated code release, though Appendix B gives a detailed three-step reproduction guide with prompts, masks, and hyperparameters.

evidence: Abstract & Section 1: reads four signal families from a single forward pass of a frozen model; explicitly 'a predictive measurement rather than a mechanistic localization'
Section 4.2 / Table 1: BEATRICE best on almost every column (e.g., .932/.826 with-context ID test vs best baseline SAPLMA .892/.744); text admits sampling baselines overtake on closed-book TriviaQA
Appendix D Table 6: paired bootstrap vs strongest of 23 baselines significant (p≤.007) on all four with-context columns and closed-book ID; closed-book OOD not significant, TQA Δ=-.046
Appendix A: label quality check — blind human re-annotation of 100 items agrees 98%, Cohen's κ=0.96; consensus filter discards 2.3%
Section 4.3 / Table 2 & Appendix D Table 7: fusion champion beats hidden-only encoder in every column, significantly on held-out single-hop sets (+.016 to +.021 AUROC)
Appendix H Tables 12-13: zero-shot transfer to real E5-retrieved context, BEATRICE first at .891 AUROC (+.039) on Qwen and .911 (+.064) on Gemma
Appendix K: full pipeline re-run on Gemma 4; closed-book-encoder benefit is base-model dependent (nine of Gemma's ten best combos carry none); sampling methods collapse to/below chance
Appendix B / Algorithm 1: full training details (AdamW 2e-4, batch 512, greedy selection δ=5e-4, layer-17 sweep) and judge/rewrite prompts in Appendix A; no code/data availability statement found

Appendix E Table 8 & Section 4.3: answer-span ablation most damaging (e.g., with-context TQA -.027 AUROC), supporting the answer-span localization claim, though main-text '0.01 closed-book' understates TQA -.032

Appendix I Table 14: PGIR leads macro EM (.408) and F1 (.484) at <4 generations/query, but SeaKR overtakes on the two hardest multi-hop sets at 13.63 generations — limitation stated plainly in Section 5.2
llm_evaluation.rationale: Core in-scope LLM methodology: probing frozen-LLM internal signals (hidden states, token probabilities, residual-stream, attention) for answer-correctness detection, tied to adaptive retrieval (PGIR). Preference relevance is high via LLM, interpretability, RAG, and evaluation matches. Novelty is moderate: the families are individually established (Azaria-Mitchell, INSIDE, Lookback-Lens, etc.); the contribution is unifying four families under early/late fusion with greedy selection and a predictive 'anatomy' study, plus a retrieval controller — solid but incremental. Rigor is strong: 23 re-implemented baselines across three tiers, validation-only design, 3-seed means, paired bootstrap with Holm correction, and honest reporting of losses (closed-book OOD not significant; Bayesian SE wins TriviaQA by -.046, Appendix D). Evidence is extensive and internally consistent (Table 1 matches Appendix C/D numbers), with gold-context caveats addressed by a real-retrieval test (Appendix H) and a second-backbone replication (Appendix K) that also honestly reports base-model dependence of the closed-book-encoder benefit and collapse of sampling baselines on Gemma. Generalizability is bounded to English open-domain QA and correctness detection; reproducibility is good on hyperparameters/prompts/algorithm (Appendix A/B) but no code or data release is stated. Minor issues: LLM-judge labels validated only on 100 human items, and main-text span-ablation deltas ('about 0.02/0.01 AUROC') slightly understate Table 8 values.

evidence: Section 3: 'We evaluate nine decoder-only checkpoints: Qwen-2.5-1.5B/7B, Gemma-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Llama-2-7B, Llama-3-8B, Llama-3.2-1B, Mistral-7B-v0.3, and Mistral-Small-24B-Base-2501', evaluated on OpenWebText and WikiText-103.
Appendix B.3: 'All 28 saved numerical parity checks pass, with maximum NLL discrepancy 5.76x10^-7', with recorded H100/bfloat16 environment and seed 2027.
Appendix C.4 / Table 3: matched final-128-target scoring shows 5% set-size estimates growing 4.12-6.63x as L goes from 256 to 2048 (e.g., Gemma-7B OWT 76 to 504) while N*/L decreases.

Section 3.3 / Table 6: BABILong qa1 with fixed annotated support shows 0.10-nat set sizes rising from 0K to 4K (Gemma 64 to 760, Llama 32 to 316), and Figure 7 reports support rank displacement ~50x and mass reduced to 0.435x (Appendix D.1).
Appendix E.1 Table 9: renormalizing retained weights reduces Gemma-7B's 5% attention-ranked estimate from 226 to 7, showing aggregation dependence.
Appendix C.2 Table 1: Spearman correlations between geometric F_N and NLL degradation weaken or flip sign after excluding N<=4, supporting the paper's qualified interpretation.

Reproducibility Statement: 'The accompanying source archive contains the manuscript and figure assets. Raw per-document measurements, experiment code, and environment manifests are needed to independently reproduce the empirical summaries.'
Section 4: authors state experiments 'do not demonstrate an inference speedup' and the conditional theory's assumptions 'have not been verified for the tested models'.
llm_evaluation.rationale: In-scope LLM interpretability/efficiency study of self-attention: measures an 'effective attention set size' via Top-N attention deletion across nine decoder-only LLMs (Qwen, Gemma, Llama, Mistral), with controlled BABILong competition experiments, context-length sweeps, renormalization controls, and conditional theory with proofs. Core relevance to LLMs, transformers, interpretability, and long context; no domain-application drift. Novelty is a solid but incremental extension of the authors' prior geometric token-selection work and existing attention-sink/sparse-attention literature, though the functional loss-based measurement and aggregation controls are distinctive. Rigor is exceptionally high: formal recovery bounds, hash-seeded sampling, adaptive threshold search, 95% bootstrap/Wilson uncertainty, and numerical parity checks (max NLL discrepancy 5.76e-7, Appendix B.3), plus unusually candid caveats (e.g., geometry-loss correlations can flip sign when N<=4 excluded, Table 1). Evidence is strong and multi-model but estimates are conditional on evaluated sizes, the useful set is unobserved, some BABILong crossings remain unresolved, and the 24B run mixes 8-bit precision. Generalizes plausibly across decoder LLMs but only four lengths/tasks and 50-document samples. Reproducibility protocols are exhaustive, yet the archive reportedly contains only manuscript/figures, with code and raw measurements noted as still needed.

links.title: Context Language Models

evidence: Abstract: claims 11.4% higher accuracy with 21.5% fewer FLOPs on BrowseComp-Plus and 65% greater improvement on a 24-hour agent-swarm task

Section 5.1.1: CLM scores 59.4% on BrowseComp-Plus at 32K context limit, exceeding Codex-style summarization by 11.4% relative with 21.5% fewer prefix-reuse FLOPs; matches TB2.1 accuracy using 70% of its FLOPs

Section 4.2: defines success-gated efficiency advantage A_eff over successful GRPO trajectories using prefix-reuse FLOPs; Table 2: RL improves Qwen3.5-9B from 28.8% to 42.5% on BCP at 1.34 vs 2.19 PFLOPs/question for the trained summary harness

Section 3 and Appendix D: ContextBench diagnostic (Needle Retention, Sudoku Sketchpad, KV Store, Log Triage) decouples context management from reasoning; 'none of the existing methods performs perfectly' at up to 24x context pressure (Figure 2)

Appendix B: SCR patch to SGLang reuses cached states of surviving tokens beyond the matched prefix with K=6 cap; sensitivity analysis on 64 BCP questions (Figure 13); Figure 14 shows 5.3 of 7.8 points of reuse come from reasoning-token stripping

Appendix E: evaluation details — all 830 BCP questions with Qwen3.5-27B judge at temperature 0, method-specific skills 'released with the benchmark', one run per method on math optimization, three seeds for EdgeBench-10

Section 6: discusses safety risk of editable context (prompt injection persisting via compaction summaries, citing OpenAI 2026b); Appendix G probes limited context-length awareness with bucketed token estimates
Section 5.1.2/Table 1: CLM beats OpenEvolve on all four math optimization problems with Claude 4.6 Sonnet, but with 'one run per method' (Appendix E)
llm_evaluation.rationale: Highly on-preference LLM/agent methodology paper: model-controlled context management ('context as a file'), stepwise GRPO RL with a success-gated efficiency advantage, in-context skill evolution, and a serving contribution (Suffix Cache Reuse in SGLang), evaluated on coding, deep-research, and long-horizon agentic tasks. Core idea is an incremental extension of a well-populated line (RLMs, MEM1, ACM, Self-Compact, MemGPT) that the paper itself frames as the 'limit' of increasing model autonomy; SCR resembles prior non-prefix cache reuse (PIE, CacheBlend) applied to agent contexts. Rigor is above average: shared Mini-SWE-Agent backbone, original baseline implementations with comparable method-specific skills, held-out splits and bootstrap CIs for steering/evolution, K-sensitivity ablation for SCR, reward ablations, and a size comparison (Qwen3.5-9B vs 27B) showing gains scale with model capability. Deductions: several experiments are single-run (math optimization, 24h Software World), key results live in figures rather than tables, and the largest gains depend on frontier/proprietary models; code URL is claimed but not verifiable from the text. Internal quantitative claims are consistent (abstract 11.4%/21.5% matches Section 5.1.1; 28.8->42.5 matches abstract's 47.6% relative).

links.title: You Cannot Pick a Provider From the Price List: Market-Aware Routing for Open-Weight LLM Inference

evidence: Section 3 / Table 2: median within-cell price-accuracy Spearman correlation is +0.05 vs. price-latency -0.61, negative in 21/21 benchmark-scale cells, showing price predicts speed but not quality.

Section 5 / Table 18: measured-map router achieves 94% mean accuracy at 1.57x cheapest cost with 0% below-floor, vs. premium routing at 3.67x cost with 17% below-floor; Appendix H shows OOS below-floor rises to 22.2% under a 2-point margin, quantifying map aging.

Section 7 / Table 6: 36-hour live deployment on Llama-3.3-70B across 12 providers served 538 queries with 130 probes, moving traffic from a $1.04/M anchor to a $0.21/M certified endpoint for 63.7% serving-cost reduction at 88.3% accuracy; the text notes no quality slip occurred, so slip detection was not live-validated.

Appendix U: TOST equivalence established in only 4/17 cells and CI-supported savings fall from 55% to 46%, with point-estimate median CI gap of 6.7 points at n~150 - a candid account of sampling-power limits.

Appendix A: limitations state all measurements traverse a single aggregator from one client location, claims are attribution-agnostic, and detector comparisons use a single Llama-3.3-70B/GSM8K replay cell; no code or artifact availability is claimed anywhere in the document.

Appendix M / Table 23: 40-seed component control with a matched monitor isolates certification (cold-start exposure 0.00-0.02% vs. 6.10% periodic) from monitoring (0.23-0.57% vs. 17.30% periodic), with probe-spend reductions of 8-23x.
llm_evaluation.rationale: Core LLM-systems work squarely within the preference profile: open-weight LLM inference routing (LLM 2.5), serving/latency/cost optimization (Inference & Serving, Scaling & Efficiency), bandit-based online decision-making, and reliability/safety framing. The provider-selection axis after model choice is a genuinely novel formulation (inverse bandit with fail-safe certification), supported by unusually careful methodology: multi-wave measurement, out-of-sample sweeps, component controls over 40 seeds, TOST/Newcombe confidence checks, and honest negative results (Appendix T falsified prediction; Appendix U underpowered equivalence tests). Evidence is strong but partly bound to one aggregator, one client location, replay-simulated drift, and a single live run that validates cold-start migration rather than slip detection; no code/data release is claimed. Generalizability of the framework is good, empirical transfer beyond the measured market is less certain, and exact replication is inherently difficult for a time-varying market.

links.title: Authority Bias in Language Models: Source Deference and User Agreement Are Not Interchangeable

evidence: Abstract: a verified-source note endorsing a wrong answer flips 45–88% of baseline-correct responses in seven of eight models; compliance rises with how authoritative the note sounds.

Section 4.3 / Table 4: source-direction removal reduces source-cued compliance by −69.6 pp (Qwen3.5 L5), −77.5 pp (GPT-OSS L16), −64.3 pp (OLMo-3.1 L22) with 10,000-sample paired bootstrap CIs, while user removal shows the reverse preference.

Section 4.4 / Table 5: separately fitted attribution patch moves compliance bidirectionally (e.g., −30.5/+32.0 pp for GPT-OSS on 512 held-out items) with all paired intervals excluding zero; Appendix H shows robustness across five layers, three wordings, two cue positions, and dose response.

Section 4.5 / Appendix E: authority direction is nearly orthogonal to the assistant axis (|cos| ≤ 0.06) and weakly overlaps the NRC-VAD valence/arousal plane (≤0.103), with causal controls showing removal effects persist outside both planes.

Section 6 Limitations: confidence intervals at strongest-sweep settings do not account for layer/strength selection; Appendix B concedes some held-out item-level outputs were not retained and OLMo-2 L16 assistant-removal runs were not reconciled.

Appendix L: Gemma-4 audit shows the fitted direction tracks endorsement presence (probe AUROC 0.53–0.60) but the 10.6% steering effect is not robust (clean rerun 1.7%), and removal changes compliance by only −2.9 pp.

llm_evaluation.rationale: Strongly in-scope: trains a small LLM advisor (Qwen3-8B) with GRPO plus selective feedback-conditioned self-distillation to steer frozen frontier LLM executors (Gemini, Claude) on multi-turn tool-use benchmarks, hitting LLM, agents/tool-use, and RL/alignment preferences directly. Novelty is moderate: advisor models, feedback-conditioned self-distillation (SDPO, DistIL, HERO, HinT-SD), and paired-contrast selection (RLCSD, OCSD, PBSD, RLSD) are acknowledged close precedents; the distinct contributions are applying paired with/without-advice scoring of a recorded executor response to gate advisor supervision, donor-advice threshold calibration, an abstention bypass, and a stylized two-teacher theory separating supervision composition from exposure. llm_evaluation.rationale: Strongly in-scope LLM/RAG methodology study: reproduces six open-source RAG-based vulnerability detection systems under open-weight inference, runs a unified PrimeVul Paired benchmark with 22 open-weight models (7 families, 3B-32B), and adds a component-level decomposition (input abstraction, knowledge retrieval, detection). Strong preference fit (LLMs, inference/serving, efficiency; UCB/bandit-style acquisition). Novelty is moderate: the economic framing and metrics are fresh, but the machinery (UCB acquisition, two-way ridge prior, shrinkage, residual ridge predictor) is classical and sparse/partial-feedback routing baselines already exist. Appendix G: built on sierra-research/tau2-bench v1.0.0 commit 8ebb749 (MIT), temperatures and serving configs specified; tables regenerated deterministically from graded trajectory files, but no explicit code/data release statement

llm_evaluation.rationale: Highly on-preference: an agentic-benchmark evaluation paper measuring LLM user simulators against their stated contracts, with frozen-agent controlled experiments, tool-call analysis, and implications for multi-turn RL. The angle—scoring user-proxy fidelity to the benchmark's own user specification rather than human realism—is a genuine complement to prior simulator-reliability work, supported by a large rubric set (2,141 criteria), a judge-free gold-action probe, cost-fidelity frontier, and unusually candid limitations. Main weaknesses: UFS is LLM-judged by the same model that generated the rubrics (generator=grader, Claude Opus 4.8), the manual audit is single-rater, non-blinded, and tiny (10 tasks + 50 judgments), one rollout per task with no variance estimates or confidence intervals, no second frozen agent, and no explicit code/data release despite deterministic-regeneration claims. Scoped to one benchmark family and one agent, limiting generalizability; judged numbers without human agreement statistics cap evidence strength.

links.title: ContextRender: From Execution Dependencies to Agent Context

evidence: Abstract: ContextRender outperforms evaluated baselines at a 6K history budget, 'reducing mean inference cost by 10.2%-32.2% relative to Full history'.

Section 4.1: evaluation on AppWorld (all 168 Test-Normal and 417 Test-Challenge tasks) and 8-objective QA (100 tasks) against five budgeted baselines (Prune, Compact LLM, Recency+Summary, Semantic Retrieval, ACON) plus Full history.

Section 4.2 and Appendix B.1: three execution models (GPT-4.1, Muse Glimmer 30B, DeepSeek V4 Pro); 'Each method is executed once per task' with temperature 0.0 and seed 42; no variance estimates or significance tests are reported.

Table 1 / Table 6: ContextRender is below Full history in two of nine settings (AppWorld Normal GPT-4.1 -2.3%, AppWorld Challenge DeepSeek -0.9%), and the reuse ablation gain is 4.1% relative TGC / 4.5% relative F1 (Section 4.4, Table 2).

Appendix A.2: TFA extraction uses pattern '[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9_.\-]{4,}' with exact case-sensitive whole-token matching; the paper states it 'does not establish a dependency on the particular value needed by an upcoming operation'.
Appendix D (Table 9): runtime adapters demonstrated for five runtimes (opencode, AppWorld ReAct, ACON UnifiedAgent, OpenClaw, Meta ARE default agent).

No code, dataset, or artifact availability statement appears anywhere in the paper; implementation is in the Jac language (Section 3.4), and evaluation depends on proprietary APIs (gpt-4.1, text-embedding-3-small).
llm_evaluation.rationale: Highly on-topic for the stated preferences: a systems method for LLM agent context management on long-horizon tool-use tasks (Agents & Tool Use 2.5, Long Context & Memory 1.8, LLMs 2.5, Inference & Serving 1.5). Novelty is moderate: the 'observed reuse' signal from Tool-Flow Analysis is a genuinely new selection signal versus recency/relevance/compaction baselines (ACE, PACE, Sculptor, ACON), but the mechanism is a heuristic regex value extraction with exact case-sensitive matching combined linearly with recency and embedding relevance. Evaluation is solid: two benchmarks (AppWorld 168+417 tasks, 8-objective QA 100 tasks), three execution models, five budgeted baselines plus full-history reference, signal ablations, budget sweep, and unusually careful cost accounting with honest protocol appendices. Weaknesses: single run per task (temperature 0, seed 42) with no variance or significance testing, gains over Full history are sometimes small or negative (e.g., -2.3% and -0.9% TGC in two of nine settings, Table 1), the ablation gain from reuse is modest (+4.1% relative TGC), and the recall metric is an acknowledged lexical proxy that 'does not establish causal dependency' (Appendix B.4). Hyperparameters (lambda=0.3, gamma=0.2, equal weights) are fixed without tuning or sensitivity analysis. Generalizability is decent (five runtime adapters, three models) but the identifier-based matching relies on information locality and may not transfer to paraphrased reuse or non-English/value-poor domains. No code or artifact release is stated, and the Jac implementation is niche, limiting reproducibility despite detailed appendices.

primary_link.title: ContextRender: From Execution Dependencies to Agent Context

papers.summary: LLM agents performing long-horizon tasks accumulate tool results that later steps may need. Passing the full history to every invocation is costly even when it fits within the context window, while reducing it risks omitting needed information. Existing context management methods can overlook how earlier tool results are used in subsequent execution, leaving needed information out of context. We introduce ContextRender, which manages context through a persistent graph of execution dependencies.

llm_evaluation.rationale: An in-scope LLM-methodology paper on inference-time self-assessment for local deployment: hidden-state probes decide compute allocation (CoT vs direct, model size) and deferral to a human. Highly relevant to LLM inference/efficiency, CoT routing, selective prediction, and probing preferences. Generalizability is plausible for MoE-based diffusion LLMs (e.g., LLaDA-MoE) but untested beyond tiny backbones; code is promised in supplementary material with detailed hyperparameters, but no public release is confirmed. Score: 0.4*0.75 + 0.15*0.7 + 0.15*0.65 + 0.15*0.65 + 0.1*0.6 + 0.05*0.6 ≈ 0.69.

evidence: Abstract: SDG 'has a small effective dimensionality (~10 dimensions for Ministral 3 (3B))' and the model performs dimensionality reduction in early layers.
Sec 4.1 Ablation: 'Ablating the top 15 dimensions of the SDG decreases model accuracy by 12.9%, boosting them increases accuracy by 3.9%, whereas ablating a random subspace has a negligible effect.'
Sec 5.2, Eqs. (9)-(12): linear self-attention with chosen W_KQ/W_OV implements a gradient step minimizing Gram error E(Z), with local exponential convergence O(exp(-4*eta*lambda_M*l)).

Appendix C.2: numerical validation under causal masking, softmax, normalization, and three initializations reaches relative Gram error below 1e-5; causal masking slows convergence but does not prevent it.
Sec 5.1/Fig 4 (Right): 'random label assignment has close to no effect during the formation phase of Text SDG', ruling out supervision-driven compression during formation.
Appendix B.3 Table 5: effective dimension of Vision SDG depends on training domain (Textures 9.71, Aircraft 6.57, all-10-datasets 9.69), an honest caveat to the 'shared 10D' claim.
Appendix E Table 8: Text SDG effective dimension 7.46-10.28 across Ministral 3 (3B/8B), Qwen 3.5 (4B/9B), and Qwen 3 (4B).
Sec 6 Table 2: SDG ablation hurts classification benchmarks (e.g., -17.0 Matching-classification split) but improves matching benchmarks (e.g., +6.5 VLGuard), delimiting scope of the geometry's role.
Limitations: 'Because our theoretical circuit assumes linear non-causal attention, it does not explain how LVLMs approximate it' and average pooling 'is a simplification'.

Reproducibility statement: 'The code is included in the supplementary material for reproducibility and will be publicly released'; Sec B.1 specifies single A100 80GB, ~3h20m training, full optimizer settings.
Sec 4.2 Table 1: staged ablations (Text SDG at l*-1: -3.2, Vision SDG at l*-1: -6.4, vision-to-text attention: -5.2, Text SDG at l*: -11.4) support the two-step formation circuit.
llm_evaluation.rationale: A mechanistic-interpretability study of in-context learning inside LVLM/LLM decoders: it identifies a shared ~10-dimensional linearly separable subspace (SDG), gives a linear-attention theory of in-context PCA-like dimensionality reduction with a convergence proof, and supports claims with controlled interventions. Strongly matches Interpretability (1.8), Multimodal AI (1.8), ICL/prompting (1.5), and Transformer Architecture (1.2), and partially LLMs (2.5), but misses the heaviest preference clusters (Japanese LLM, reasoning, agents), capping relevance at ~0.6. Not pure computer vision: the object of study is the language-model decoder circuit, so the out-of-scope cap does not apply. Novelty is solid: claimed first showing linear transformers perform in-context dimensionality reduction, and a two-step vision-to-text formation circuit, though closely adjacent to von Oswald/Ahn gradient-descent-in-attention and existing subspace work. Rigor is high (Lean-verified proof, numerical validation relaxing causal/softmax/normalization assumptions, random-subspace controls, random-label control, 1000-task averages, 5 models), with honest limitations that the theoretical non-causal linear circuit is only indirectly matched in trained models and that effective dimension varies with setup/domain (6.57-11.08). Evidence is quantitative and intervention-based but the mechanism link remains correlational-plus-ablation rather than direct identification. Generalizability is moderate: consistent across five models and 10 vision datasets plus SST-2 and 7 multimodal benchmarks, but classification-centric, LVLM-family-only, and matching tasks show the opposite SDG effect. Reproducibility is good: code in supplementary with release promise, full hyperparameters (B.1), and public datasets.

evidence: Abstract: SOMA N=2 with 64 perturbations reaches 1.76 test nats/byte at 150 aggregate GPU-hours vs 2.00-2.11 for monolithic SPSA (64/256/1024 perturbations) and 2.21 for EGGROLL at ~8.44M parameters.

Section 5 and Appendix F, Proposition 1: independent losses reduce relative gradient variance to ~1/N on a separable objective; Figure 11 shows 4.02x measured error reduction vs 4.00x predicted on SOMA N=4.
Section 6, External-corpus evaluation and Table 9: frozen checkpoints near 150 GPU-hours score 2.07 (SOMA N=2) vs 2.25-2.36 (monolithic SPSA) and 2.49 (EGGROLL) on WikiText-103.

Appendix I, Table 5: BPTT reaches lower ensemble validation loss at every tested budget (e.g., 1.0198 vs 2.1237 at 50 GPU-hours for N=1), explicitly showing no advantage over backpropagation for these recipes.

Appendix J: paired continuations with fixed weights, data, perturbations and compute show independent losses improve test loss by 0.035 nats/byte after 1,000 updates across three seeds, with variance reduced 3.19-4.64x.

Section 8, Tables 12-13: SOMA N=256 achieves 2.36M tokens/s vs 257k for SOMA N=8 (9.19x including routing) at lower test loss (1.68 vs 1.71), but uses 59.9x more aggregate training compute; Table 13 notes the endpoint comparison does not establish a matched-duration loss advantage.
Section 9 and Appendix O: limitations include one byte-level corpus, 8.44M parameters, mostly single-seed scaling runs, ~700 passes per shard at N=256, and a fixed tf-idf router that does not adapt.

Reproducibility statement and Appendix L: release of all training/evaluation code, checkpoints, plotted CSVs, frozen dataset manifest, and a CPU evaluation package with pinned dependencies and expected scores.
llm_evaluation.rationale: A methodology paper on zero-order (backprop-free) pretraining of language models via sharded LSTM expert ensembles (SOMA). Topic relevance is moderate: it matches LLM/pretraining, training-optimization, and scaling/efficiency preferences, but not the highest-weighted areas (reasoning, agents, Japanese NLP), and the models are tiny (8.44M params), limiting 'large language model' relevance. Novelty is solid: applying CBTM-style sharding to ZO pretraining with independent losses appears new, with a clean 1/N variance proposition and a novel inference-throughput analysis of heavily sharded ZO ensembles, though it recombines known ingredients (SPSA/ES + branch-train-merge). Rigor is high: formal proofs (Appendix F), variance predictions verified empirically (4.02x measured vs 4.00x predicted), a three-seed equal-tuning comparison (Table 7), paired controlled continuations (Appendix J), overlap-screened test set (Appendix L), and unusually honest reporting that BPTT beats ZO at every tested budget (Table 5). Evidence strength is good but bounded: headline comparisons are at ~150 GPU-hours with different update counts, the EGGROLL baseline is a GRU-based reproduction, most scaling runs are single-seed, and all conclusions are at 8.44M scale on one corpus family (plus WikiText-103 frozen eval). Generalizability is limited by explicit scope restrictions: byte-level LSTM experts, one fixed tf-idf router, single corpus, and unknown behavior at larger scale where ZO variance grows with dimension. Reproducibility is strong: detailed hyperparameters, compute accounting (Table 3), and specific release claims (code, checkpoints, CSVs, manifests, CPU evaluation package), though release could not be independently verified from the document.

links.title: CompOrca: Corpus-Scale Compliance Labelling of Instruction-Tuning Data

evidence: Abstract: unanimous compliance/noncompliance labels are '97.3% and 86.7% precise' against 450 human-annotated examples; 'Published refusal-detection methods recall only between 0.4% and 94.1%'.

Section 3: five independent passes of LongCat-2.0 (1x T=0, 4x T=0.7); Table 1: 94.75% unanimous compliance, 1.28% unanimous noncompliance, 3.97% nonunanimous; '21,169,615 classifications over 15.19B tokens'.
Section 4.2: human-human agreement 96.7% [92.4, 98.6], Cohen's kappa=0.933; unanimous labels agree with human labels on 97.2% of rows reweighted (CI [94.5, 99.2]).
Table 3 (Section 5): methods span 0.4% recall (Do-Not-Answer Longformer) to 94.1% (WildGuard) on human labels; WildGuard corpus-wide precision only 19.5% at 1.28% base rate.

Limitations: 'Five passes of one model improve self-consistency instead of correctness'; 4/150 sampled compliance rows human-labelled noncompliance imply 'a corpus-reweighted recall of 30.4%... CompOrca provides a subset of the corpus's noncompliance, rather than a complete enumeration'; validation set labelled by one author with a 150-row second annotation.
Appendix A-C: full judge prompt reproduced, codebook with 12 cases, and Appendix B Table 4 gives inference configuration; dataset and gold annotations released at HuggingFace links in Section 7.
llm_evaluation.rationale: A corpus-scale data-labelling contribution squarely within LLM scope: refusal/noncompliance labelling of the 4.2M-row OpenOrca instruction-tuning corpus using a five-pass LLM-as-judge protocol, with comparisons against six published refusal-detection methods. Strong preference match (LLMs, AI Safety, Alignment/RLHF data, Red Teaming & Evaluation, Data & Datasets) and not a domain application. Novelty is moderate: multi-pass judging for self-consistency is borrowed (Section 2 cites Wang et al. 2023), so the contribution is primarily scale and the first full row-level release, not methodological novelty. Rigor is reasonable but constrained: a 450-row human validation set with double annotation on 150 rows (Section 4.2), bootstrap CIs, corpus reweighting, and a second-judge check (Section 4.1), yet labels were authored mainly by one annotator who also wrote the judge prompt and codebook, and the Limitations section concedes unanimous compliance labels have only ~30.4% corpus-reweighted recall for noncompliance, i.e., the release is a high-precision subset, not an enumeration. Evidence strength is adequate with internally consistent tables (Tables 1-3), but the small, single-annotator validation set caps confidence in corpus-wide claims; honesty about incompleteness is a plus. Generalizability is moderate since findings on substring-list failure (12.6% precision, 6.3% recall) and single-pass judge instability (52-60% of flags fail unanimity) likely transfer, but labels are tied to one corpus, one judge model, and a broad noncompliance definition. Reproducibility is strong: judge prompt (Appendix A), inference config (Appendix B), codebook (Appendix C), dataset and gold labels released on HuggingFace, and the judge is open-weight, though it was served via a stealth endpoint.

Table A4 (Appendix A.3.3): MMSI-Bench overall 29.33±0.99 across three random seeds

llm_evaluation.rationale: Core methodology is an LLM multi-agent coding pipeline (Qwen3-Coder-30B agents with Architect/Coder/Reviewer/Refiner roles and a geometric tool API) for synthetic spatial VQA data, followed by SFT/LoRA of Qwen2.5-VL models - strongly matching Agents & Tool Use, Code & Programming, LLMs, Reasoning, and Multimodal AI preferences, though it lacks any Japanese NLP content and the domain is spatial VQA rather than pure language modeling. Rigor is reasonably solid (topology and generator-capacity ablations, direct-LLM-annotation comparison, matched-hyperparameter baselines, seed-stability table, error analysis, limitations section) but weakened by suspicious generator model names (Qwen3.5-9B, Gemini3.5-Flash), VSI-Bench evaluation restricted to the multiple-choice subset in the main table, small 100-seed ablations, and admitted absence of error bars for headline results. Generalizability is a strength (indoor-to-outdoor transfer, four+ benchmarks, backbone transfer). links.title: Pretraining Latent Information Feedback Transformers with Teacher Supervision

evidence: Abstract: 'Experiments with pretrained models ranging from 135M to 1B parameters show that LIFT consistently outperforms standard Transformers and baselines on language modeling, downstream reasoning tasks, and procedural tasks under token-matched budget.'

§5.2 / Table 1: 'At matched tokens, LIFT is ahead on every metric at every scale: perplexity drops by 5–5.5%, and it wins 33 of the 36 downstream benchmark comparisons'; compute-matched Transformers train on >40% more tokens yet LIFT 'keeps the lead on every metric at 350M and 1B'.

§4 Results: two-layer LIFT solves 12-step S5 sequences at 100% accuracy 'even when the states come from a Transformer teacher that itself fails at that length (3%)', extrapolating to 96% at N=32 and 65% at N=64; §C.1 shows Transformer gains saturate by 20× budget.

§D.1: 'At 135M, LIFT improves perplexity over the compute-matched Transformer by 0.47±0.08'; the no-teacher self-state variant ties it (+0.01±0.05), so 'the teacher thus accounts for 98% of LIFT's gain', and input-only (λ=0) falls behind—supporting the mechanism claims with controls.

Appendix B.2–B.4: complete configs (OLMo 2 codebase/data, WSD schedule, k=1024, τ=1.5, λ=1.5, data mix percentages); footnote 1 releases code and trained models at https://github.com/dortirosh1/LIFT/.

§C.4 Table 10 and Table 14 give three-seed mean±sd; §7 acknowledges teacher-architecture/vocabulary limits and the unexplored beyond-teacher-budget regime; §F.1 notes the compute-matched accounting inadvertently favored baselines by ~2.5% more tokens.
llm_evaluation.rationale: Core LLM methodology paper: modifies Transformer pretraining to add a teacher-forced latent feedback channel, directly matching the highest-weight preferences (LLMs, Transformer architecture, reasoning, training/scaling). Not a domain application; clearly in scope. Novelty is solid but incremental over a dense related-work field (Coconut, T2MLR, PonderLM, CoCoMix, Thinking States); the specific combination—teacher-forced next-token distributions as pretraining inputs with self-state adaptation—is credibly claimed as first (Table 20). Rigor is high: token- and compute-matched baselines, distillation and channel-off controls isolating the mechanism, ablations over teacher use, channel width k, trunk vs. adaptation phase, and teacher strength, three seeds at 135M plus seed tables, paired bootstrap intervals, and FLOPs/memory accounting. Evidence is strong at small scale; the 350M/1B results rest on single seeds and several matched-compute downstream gaps are honestly reported as within noise. Generalizability is good across 135M–1B and two setups but bounded by shared-tokenizer teachers and OLMo 2/SmolLM2 backbones; limitations are acknowledged (§7). Reproducibility is strong: code and models released, exhaustive hyperparameters in Appendices A–B. Aggregate ≈0.86.

primary_link.title: Pretraining Latent Information Feedback Transformers with Teacher Supervision

top5.summary: Transformer language models (LMs) are feed-forward: deep-layer representations are never fed back to shallower layers, and the only pathway for information to flow downward across generation steps is the decoded token. This narrow channel forces models to recompute intermediate results and to discard alternative continuations. links.title: LeapQuant: Efficient Linear Attention with Accurate Recurrent State Quantization

evidence: Abstract & Section 4.2: 'With 8-bit quantization, LeapQuant achieves accuracy on par with the FP32 baseline across the 12 model–task pairs'; Table 1 shows Ours 8-bit avg 75.5 equal to FP32 75.5 while BF16 per-step drops Qwen3.5-9B AIME to 72.1.
Section 4.4 Table 2: staged ablation raises INT8 AIME from 7.1 (per-step) to 82.4 (+per-window), 86.6 (+Compensator Tokens), 87.9 (+smoothing) at 2.52x kernel speedup.

Section 4.3: kernel speedups of 2.68x/3.95x/4.25x (GDN) and 2.41x/3.38x/3.64x (KDA) at batch 512; state stored at 1.19 bytes/element vs 4 (3.4x traffic reduction); end-to-end memory cut 41-56% with prefix caching.

Section 4.1: baselines span FP8/INT8/MXFP/NVFP4/MXFP4 plus adapted KVQuant, QuaRot, TurboQuant; 'Due to limited hardware resources, we run only 8-layer versions of Qwen3.8-Flash and GLM-5.3-Flash ... use them only for efficiency measurements.'
Appendix A Table 4: the general update form covers Linear Attention, RetNet, Mamba2, GLA/RWKV6/HGRN2, DeltaNet, Gated DeltaNet, KDA, RWKV7, DeltaProduct, supporting architectural generalizability.
Section 4.1 states implementation in vLLM with TileLang kernels and Table 6 lists full sampling parameters, but no code or artifact availability claim appears anywhere in the paper.
llm_evaluation.rationale: Core LLM-inference efficiency paper: training-free quantization of the recurrent state in linear-attention hybrid LLMs (GDN/KDA), directly matching the LLM, transformer-architecture/SSM, scaling-efficiency, and inference-serving preferences. Novelty is solid rather than groundbreaking: per-window quantization exploits the known chunkwise unrolling of linear attention, and Compensator Tokens are a rank-one outlier-absorption scheme in the spirit of SVDQuant/GEAR, though the reuse of the delta-rule update path and the error-accumulation analysis (Appendix B.1) are new for recurrent states. Rigor is strong: 5 models, 5 benchmarks, 8/6/4-bit comparisons against FP8/INT8/MXFP/KVQuant/QuaRot/TurboQuant (Appendix C), three-seed averaging, staged ablations (Table 2), and p/r sweeps (Table 3); deducted for no variance reporting and for baselines that must be adapted rather than purpose-built, plus 8-layer proxy models for two efficiency-only evaluations (Section 4.1). Evidence is internally consistent (Table 1 avg 75.5 matches FP32; ablation endpoints match Table 1), though speedup figures cannot be verified from text. Generalizes across the recurrence family (Appendix A Table 4) and is calibration-free, but is specific to delta-rule-style linear attention states. No explicit code/artifact release is stated, lowering reproducibility despite detailed hyperparameters (p=16, r=4) and Table 6 sampling settings.

links.title: EngiWorld: What Can Frontier Agents Deliver in Professional Engineering Environments?

evidence: Abstract: '1,301 expert-curated tasks spanning 6 engineering domains (CAD, CAE, CAM, BIM, EDA, and 3D visualization) and 26 professional software platforms'; 'the strongest model achieves an EngiScore of only 44.3, and just 3.6% of multi-software attempts succeed.'

Section 3.4 / Section 4.1: artifact-centric evaluation with equations (1)-(3); evaluation of seven models on 'the same stratified subset of 300 tasks, comprising 152 CLI-interface tasks and 148 GUI-interface tasks' in a zero-shot setting.

Appendix B.3, Table B.3: verifier validation — all 96 reference artifacts accepted, 40+40 alternative-solver and 5 alternative-design submissions accepted, 21 empty and 21 metrics-only submissions all rejected; text notes 'tolerance-boundary tests are outside the completed audit populations.'

Section 4.3, Tables 3-4 and Figure 6: ablations on initial-image presentation (GPT GUI 15.0→31.7 with message placement), runtime image access (readimg helps Gemini, hurts Kimi), accessibility trees, resolution, and history length, with model-dependent effects explicitly acknowledged.

Section 4.4, Table D.1: failure taxonomy over 3,347 distinct failed runs — DONE with zero score 49.03%, decision-turn limit 44.79%; Table D.3 lists four verified violations in agent-declared successes (e.g., GPT-5.6 Sol left 3.698 mm3 residual material vs 0.1 mm3 allowance).

Appendix C.3, Table C.3: paired Multi-software vs Open-ended analysis — all seven models fail the Multi-software versions of tasks 02/09, while four models succeed on Open-ended task 09, isolating delivery/handoff failures from geometric capability.

Reproducibility: Appendix B.1 Table B.1 lists 37 environments with software versions and OS; Section 4.1 specifies PyAutoGUI, 1920×1080 screenshots, 15-round history, and step limits; a project page URL is given but no explicit code/task-release commitment appears in the text.
llm_evaluation.rationale: A large-scale agent benchmark evaluating seven frontier LLM/MLLM agents on professional engineering software via GUI/CLI interaction, squarely matching Agents & Tool Use and LLM preferences plus evaluation methodology. Novelty is moderate: it unifies existing ideas (OSWorld-style interaction, single-domain artifact verifiers) into a 6-domain/26-platform suite with a continuous quantitative-design score, but the methodology components are largely assembled from prior work. Rigor is solid — formal task/scoring formulation, verifier validation with reference, alternative-valid, and defective populations (Table B.3), stratified 300-task main evaluation, ablations, and a failure taxonomy — though it lacks statistical treatment, single-run evaluations, small strata (only 4 Open-ended tasks in the main eval), and an admittedly incomplete verifier audit ('tolerance-boundary tests are outside the completed audit populations'). Evidence is extensive and internally consistent (per-category scores, token/cost accounting, verified violation case studies), but no explicit code/data release statement appears beyond a project-page URL, limiting reproducibility despite detailed environment/version documentation. Findings are honestly framed as model-dependent, which caps generalizability claims.

links.title: Prompts Live on an Arc: Gaussian Curricula in Fisher--Rao Coordinates for Rollout-Efficient GRPO

evidence: Abstract/§5.2 Table 1: Arcus improves average accuracy over GRPO by 2.8–2.9 points and over dynamic sampling by 1.1–1.2 points across three backbones while generating 48–57% fewer rollouts than DS.

§3 Propositions 1–4 and Corollary 1: GRPO update is uniform in ψ=arcsin√p up to boundary ramps; zero-variance probability bounded by Gaussian layers e^{-Gψ²}+e^{-G(π/2−ψ)²}; evidence variance 1/(4n); pass@k gradients are Gaussians with mode arcsin(1/√(2k)); any fixed sampler w(ψ) ascends a derived objective F_w.
§5.3 Table 3: ablations quantify components — Gaussian over raw p −0.69, logit-space Kalman −0.96, no dead-zone factor ŷ −1.03, fixed pass@1 target −0.62, reward-feedback pacing −0.85.

Appendix B.10 Table 4: exact numerical verification of all analytic claims (e.g., Prop.1 matches Davis & Recht weight to <10⁻¹⁴; TV between H_k and Laplace kernel 0.050–0.069), produced by code/theory_checks.py.

§5.5 and Appendix F Tables 11–12, 15: gains persist on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B (+2.4 vs GRPO), Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct (+1.9), MATH pool (+2.2), and under Dr. GRPO/DAPO/RLOO losses (+1.1–1.2 over DS).
Appendix D/E Tables 5–6 plus reproducibility checklist (i)–(vi): full hyperparameters, algorithm pseudocode, seeded Gumbel noise, three training seeds; no external code-release URL stated.
Limitations section: derived for binary rewards and std-dev-normalized GRPO; experiments cover mathematical reasoning, models ≤7B, G≤16; code and agentic tasks remain untested.
llm_evaluation.rationale: Core LLM methodology paper: improves GRPO (RLVR) post-training for mathematical reasoning by deriving a Fisher–Rao arc-length coordinate for pass rates and building Arcus, a closed-form Kalman-filter prompt sampler with objective pacing. Strongly matches high-weight preferences (LLMs, reasoning, RL, training/efficiency). Novelty is solid but derivative in part: the arcsine objective of GRPO is credited to Davis & Recht (2025), and Anscombe/variance-stabilization, Kalman filtering, and Gumbel-top-k are classical; the contribution is composing them into a geometry-derived sampler that provably reshapes the implicit objective (Corollary 1) and predicts waste (Prop. 7). Rigor is high: four propositions with proofs (App. B), exact numerical checks (App. B.10, Table 4), extensive ablations isolating coordinate/kernel/pacing (Tables 3, 8), mechanism analysis, three seeds with s.d. (Table 7). Evidence is strong: best averages on all three backbones (Table 1), 48–57% fewer rollouts than DS, cost and wall-clock breakdowns (Tables 2, 6), generality across backbones, pools, and losses (Tables 11, 12, 15). Generalizability is limited by math-only binary-reward evaluation, models ≤7B, G≤16 (Limitations), though the theory formally extends to any binary verifier. Reproducibility is good (full hyperparameters, Algorithms 1–2, evaluation protocol, reproducibility checklist), but no external code-release URL is verifiable, only internal script references. Minor caution: evaluation sets like AIME (30 problems) are small, mitigated by multi-seed and multi-benchmark averaging.

llm_evaluation.rationale: Highly relevant: an LLM-safety/mechanistic-interpretability study localizing prompt-injection compliance via causal activation patching across five open models (Qwen3-4B/14B/32B, Phi-3-mini, Mistral-7B), with detection, probing, and agentic/robustness follow-ups. Novelty is solid but incremental over refusal-direction and intermediate-layer detection work (Arditi et al. 2024; Wen et al. 2025), which it explicitly positions against. Rigor is strong: control batteries (benign/compliant/norm-matched random), same-prompt analyses, sublayer decomposition, rank-k PCA, split-half subspace validation, temperature/GCG/multi-turn robustness, and public-benchmark replication with benchmark-matched donors; honest negative results (agentic single-token patching fails, MoE weak, naturalistic flip ~12%) are reported. Evidence is detailed and appropriately hedged, though the headline 77-92% figure comes from a synthetic single-turn AcmeCorp setting and labels rely on keyword matching plus an LLM judge. Generalizability is partial: the clean early-decode/late-cause dissociation holds mainly for dense non-thinking models, English-only stimuli, and peak layers vary (63-91% depth). Reproducibility is moderate: public models, system prompts, and benchmark datasets are specified, but the synthetic corpus and code are not explicitly released.
